Remarks on Exponential Stability for a Coupled System of Elasticity and Thermoelasticity with Second Sound

Manuel Rissele1,addr1 Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, P. R. China    Ya-Guang Wange2,addr2 Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Center of Applied Mathematics, MOE-LSC and SHL-MAC, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, P. R. China
Received: date / Accepted: date
Abstract

We study the large time behavior of solutions to a linear transmission problem in one space dimension. The problem at hand models a thermoelastic material with second sound confined by a purely elastic one. We shall characterize all equilibrium states of the considered system and prove that every solution approaches one designated equilibrium state with an exponential rate as time goes to infinity. Hereto, we apply methods from the theory of strongly continuous semigroups. In particular, we obtain uniform resolvent bounds for the underlying generator. This removes the largeness assumption of elastic wave speeds imposed in [Y.P. Meng and Y.G. Wang, Anal. Appl. (Singap.) 13 (2015)] for having an exponential energy decay rate when the problem only has the trivial equilibrium. In an appendix we provide a similar exponential stability result for the case where heat conduction is modeled using Fourier’s law.

Keywords: 
transmission problem thermoelasticity elasticity second sound exponential stability
MSC
35B35, 35B40, 35M33, 47D06

1 Introduction

Many interesting applications give rise to transmission problems, which are systems of differential equations with discontinuous coefficients and transmission conditions imposed on some interfaces. In this note we are concerned with a transmission problem for a coupled system of elasticity and thermoelasticity, as illustrated in Figure 1. In this work, the heat conduction in thermoelasticity obeys the Cattaneo law, which transforms the classical thermoelastic system of hyperbolic-parabolic type into the thermoelastic system with second sound, a strictly hyperbolic one, cf. [19]. We aim to develop the linear semigroup theory to re-study the long time stability analysis of this problem initiated in [13] via the Lyapunov argument. In particular, by the means of uniform resolvent bounds, we shall show that all equilibria are exponentially stable. While our motivation stems from the work [13], where only the model with Cattaneo’s law is considered, it seems to us that the same setting but with classical Fourier’s law for heat conduction has not been studied, in particular in the semigroup context, as well. For this reason, in the appendix, we also provide details on how to obtain exponential stability when Fourier’s law is employed and the thermoelastic part of the bar is modeled in the classical way. The one dimensional systems investigated here serve as toy-models for the curl-free part of considerably more complicated vectorial cases and are also of interest from the perspective of control theory.

The dynamics of the elastic-thermoelastic-elastic bar under consideration, with Cattaneo’s law for heat conduction, are modeled by the following set of coupled partial differential equations,

ut​t−a​ux​x+m​θx\displaystyle u_{tt}-au_{xx}+m\theta_{x} =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [L1,L2]×ℝ+,\displaystyle[L_{1},L_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, (1)
θt+k​qx+m​ux​t\displaystyle\theta_{t}+kq_{x}+mu_{xt} =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [L1,L2]×ℝ+,\displaystyle[L_{1},L_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}_{+},
τ​qt+q+k​θx\displaystyle\tau q_{t}+q+k\theta_{x} =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [L1,L2]×ℝ+,\displaystyle[L_{1},L_{2}]\times\mathbb{R}_{+},
vt​t−b​vx​x\displaystyle v_{tt}-bv_{xx} =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [0,L1]∪[L2,L3]×ℝ+,\displaystyle[0,L_{1}]\cup[L_{2},L_{3}]\times\mathbb{R}_{+},

with transmission conditions at the interfaces

u⁡(Li,⋅)\displaystyle u(L_{i},\cdot) =\displaystyle= v⁡(Li,⋅)\displaystyle v(L_{i},\cdot) in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } ℝ+\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{+}\,\, (i=1,2),\displaystyle(i=1,2), (2)
a​ux​(Li,⋅)\displaystyle au_{x}(L_{i},\cdot) −\displaystyle- m​θ​(Li,⋅)\displaystyle m\theta(L_{i},\cdot) =\displaystyle= b​vx​(Li,⋅)\displaystyle bv_{x}(L_{i},\cdot) in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } ℝ+\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{+}\,\, (i=1,2),\displaystyle(i=1,2),

and usual Dirichlet conditions for the displacement at the endpoints of the bar as well as for the heat flux at the insulated ends of the middle part,

q⁡(L1,⋅)\displaystyle q(L_{1},\cdot) =\displaystyle= q⁡(L2,⋅)\displaystyle q(L_{2},\cdot) =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } ℝ+,\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{+}, (3)
v⁡(0,⋅)\displaystyle v(0,\cdot) =\displaystyle= v⁡(L3,⋅)\displaystyle v(L_{3},\cdot) =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } ℝ+,\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{+},

further complemented by initial conditions

u⁡(⋅,0)=u0,ut​(⋅,0)=u1,θ⁡(⋅,0)=θ0,q⁡(⋅,0)=q0\displaystyle u(\cdot,0)=u_{0},~u_{t}(\cdot,0)=u_{1},~\theta(\cdot,0)=\theta_{0},~q(\cdot,0)=q_{0} in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [L1,L2],\displaystyle[L_{1},L_{2}], (4)
v⁡(⋅,0)=v0,vt​(⋅,0)=v1\displaystyle v(\cdot,0)=v_{0},~v_{t}(\cdot,0)=v_{1} in\displaystyle\mbox{ in } [0,L1]∪[L2,L3].\displaystyle[0,L_{1}]\cup[L_{2},L_{3}].

The unknown functions to be determined are the displacement uu, the temperature θ\theta and the heat flux qq for the middle part of the bar, while vv is the unknown displacement of the outer parts. Moreover, a,m,k,τ,b>0a,m,k,\tau,b>0 are strictly positive parameters, which are arbitrary but fixed and represent physical properties of the considered materials. The limit case τ=0\tau=0 corresponds to Fourier’s law of heat conduction, where q=−k​θxq=-k\theta_{x}, regarding which we refer to [19], some references below and the appendix. As in [13], we assume that the elastic speed b>0\sqrt{b}>0 is identical for the material in [0,L1][0,L_{1}] and [L2,L3][L_{2},L_{3}]. The problem (1)-(4) was studied in [13] by using the energy method, in which they obtained that if the initial data satisfy the constraint

∫L1L2θ0​dx+m⁡(u0​(L2)−u0​(L1))=0,\displaystyle\int_{L_{1}}^{L_{2}}\theta_{0}\,dx+m(u_{0}(L_{2})-u_{0}(L_{1}))=0, (5)

and the wave speed b\sqrt{b} is large enough in the sense of (13, (3.37) of Theorem 3.8), then the solution of the above problem decays exponentially to zero in the energy space when tt goes to infinity.

The aim of this article is to study the problem (1)-(4) by using a semigroup approach, and we shall deduce that the localized dissipation of the thermoelasticity in the equations (1)-(4) is strong enough to guarantee any stationary state of the problem (1)-(4) being exponentially stable, and the constraint (5) being equivalent to that this problem has only the trivial equilibrium.

Thus, in contrast to [13], there are two novelties at least in this paper, one is that by using the semigroup approach, without the largeness requirement of the wave speed b\sqrt{b} imposed in [13], we obtain that the solution of (1)-(4) decays to zero exponentially when the time tt goes to infinity under the assumption (5) of the initial data, the second is that any solution of this problem goes to a steady state exponentially when tt goes to infinity even without the constraint (5). Besides that, it seems that exponential stability for solutions to (1)-(4) with τ=0\tau=0 (using Fourier’s law) is likewise not available in the literature up to now, in particular from a semigroup point of view. Therefore, the discussion we provide in the appendix might be of interest as well. For cases where the thermoelastic part is located in at least one end of the bar, exponential stability has been obtained in a semilinear context with Cattaneo’s law by Sare, Muñoz Rivera & Racke [21] and with Fourier’s law by Marzocchi, Muñoz Rivera & Naso [12]. These works both employ an energy method for treating the semilinear problem directly.

The essential difference of our approach, compared to the energy functional method used in [13], is that we work in the frequency domain and study the generator of the semigroup which governs the linear dynamics. While an energy functional approach, employed for example in [1, 6, 10, 13, 14, 18, 21, 23], is beneficial in that it directly applies to some semilinear settings, there might appear disadvantages when necessary conditions for stability are desired or in cases where suitable Lyapunov type functionals are difficult to obtain. On the contrary, the linear semigroup approach offers several equivalent characterizations for exponential stability and some criteria for weaker forms such as polynomial or strong stability, which have also proven to be helpful for showing the lack of exponential stability, see for example [1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 15, 16, 20, 22, 24, 25].

Regarding (1)-(4), we shall observe below, see (9), that the generator 𝒜\mathcal{A} of the underlying semigroup allows a natural decomposition 𝒜=𝒞+ℰ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{C}+\mathcal{E} with 𝒞\mathcal{C} skew-adjoint and ℰ\mathcal{E} bounded selfadjoint. We note that therefore the dissipative effects, entering this system only through the heatflux qq, are rather weak. In particular, the spectrum of 𝒜\mathcal{A} lives in an infinite strip of thickness τ−1\tau^{-1} touching the imaginary axis, see Remark 1 and Proposition 2 below. This is due to the use of Cattaneo’s law for modeling the thermoelastic component as a hyperbolic system in order to rule out the paradox of infinite speeds of propagation, observed for classical heat diffusion models following Fourier’s law [19]. With Fourier’s law, the perturbation ℰ\mathcal{E} becomes an unbounded one, introducing some parabolic features. In both cases, the nice structure of the generator relies on the natural choice of the transmission conditions (2), which guarantee a matching of the forces at the interfaces.

+12∫L1L2(a|ux(t,x)|2+|ut(t,x)|2+|θ(t,x)|2+τ|q(t,x)|2)dx.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\int_{L_{1}}^{L_{2}}\left(a|u_{x}(t,x)|^{2}+|u_{t}(t,x)|^{2}+|\theta(t,x)|^{2}+\tau|q(t,x)|^{2}\right)\,dx.

Our main result, stated later in Theorem 3.2, can for the time being be formulated as below in Theorem 1.1. For the case of Fourier’s law we refer to Theorem A.1.

Theorem 1.1

There exist constants M,ω>0M,\omega>0 such that, for every initial datum

U0=[u0,v0,q0,θ0,u1,v1]′U_{0}=[u_{0},v_{0},q_{0},\theta_{0},u_{1},v_{1}]^{\prime}

with finite energy EU0E_{U_{0}}, the corresponding finite energy solution

U=U⁡(t,x)=[u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x),q⁡(t,x),θ⁡(t,x)]′U=U(t,x)=[u(t,x),v(t,x),q(t,x),\theta(t,x)]^{\prime}

to (1) - (4) satsifies

EU−W0​(t)≤M​e−ω​t(t≥0),E_{U-W_{0}}(t)\leq M\operatorname{e}^{-\omega t}\quad(t\geq 0),

where W0W_{0} is a stationary solution to (1) - (4) and uniquely determined by U0U_{0}.

The structure of the article at hand is as follows. In Section 2, the well-posedness of (1)-(4) is settled in the framework of strongly continuous semigroups, some spectral properties of the generator are obtained and all stationary states are characterized. Then, in Section 3, the uniform exponential stability result of Theorem 1.1 is established. Some calculations are outsourced to Section 4. Finally, some details regarding the classical model with Fourier’s law, culminating in Theorem A.1, are presented in form of an appendix.

Proposition 1

The operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} generates a strongly continuous contraction semigroup (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0} on ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Lemma 1

ℋ=ker⁡(𝒜)⊕range⁡(𝒜)\mathcal{H}=\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A})\oplus\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{A}).

Proof

The equality (12) likewise holds for 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*}. Therefore, if U∈ker⁡(A)∪ker⁡(A∗)U\in\operatorname{ker}(A)\cup\operatorname{ker}(A^{*}), then ‖q‖L2​(L1,L2)=0\|q\|_{L^{2}(L_{1},L_{2})}=0. Hence, by observing the formula for 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*} in the proof of Proposition 1 it becomes evident that ker⁡(𝒜)=ker⁡(𝒜∗)\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A})=\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A}^{*}). Indeed, 𝒜+Eτ=−𝒜∗−Eτ\mathcal{A}+E_{\tau}=-\mathcal{A}^{*}-E_{\tau}, where the operator Eτ:ℋ→ℋE_{\tau}\colon\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H} was defined above in (10). It is known that, 𝒜\mathcal{A} being densely defined, ker⁡(𝒜∗)=range⁡(𝒜)⟂\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A}^{*})=\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{A})^{\perp}. Inserting ker⁡(𝒜)=ker⁡(𝒜∗)\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A})=\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A}^{*}) concludes the proof. ∎

In this section we prove the uniform exponential stability for (1) - (4). We adopt hereto the approach from [11] and recall the following theorem from the theory of operator semigroups, see Huang [8] and Prüss [17], using here the same formulation as in (11, Theorem 1.3.1).

Proof

Due to the previous elaborations, Theorem 3.1 can be applied and implies uniform exponential stability for the semigroup (T0​(t))t≥0(T_{0}(t))_{t\geq 0} generated by 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}. We note that (T0​(t))t≥0(T_{0}(t))_{t\geq 0} is the restriction of (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0} to range(𝒜)\operatornamewithlimits{range}(\mathcal{A}). Indeed, range(𝒜)\operatornamewithlimits{range}(\mathcal{A}) is an invariant subspace of (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0} and one can see that 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}, as defined in the beginning of this section, is the part of 𝒜\mathcal{A} in range(𝒜)\operatornamewithlimits{range}(\mathcal{A}) according to the unnumbered Definition from (5, Page 60). The unnumbered proposition from (5, Page 60), noting also (5, Page 43, 5.12), can be applied in order to see that 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is the generator of the restriction of (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0} to range(𝒜)\operatornamewithlimits{range}(\mathcal{A}). The assertion of Theorem 3.2 follows now by noticing that

‖T⁡(t)​U0−W0‖ℋ\displaystyle\|T(t)U_{0}-W_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖T⁡(t)​W0−W0‖ℋ+‖T⁡(t)​V0‖ℋ\displaystyle\|T(t)W_{0}-W_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|T(t)V_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}
=\displaystyle= ‖T0​(t)​V0‖ℋ\displaystyle\|T_{0}(t)V_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}
≤\displaystyle\leq M​e−ω​t​‖V0‖ℋ\displaystyle M\operatorname{e}^{-\omega t}\|V_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}
≤\displaystyle\leq M​e−ω​t​‖U0‖ℋ,\displaystyle M\operatorname{e}^{-\omega t}\|U_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}},

for all t≥0t\geq 0. We used above that W0∈ker⁡(𝒜)W_{0}\in\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A}) and the property of a strongly continuous semigroup and its generator to commute, hence

‖dd​t​T​(t)​W0‖ℋ=‖𝒜​T​(t)​W0‖ℋ=‖T⁡(t)​𝒜​W0‖ℋ=0(t≥0),\left\|\frac{d}{dt}T(t)W_{0}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\mathcal{A}T(t)W_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|T(t)\mathcal{A}W_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=0\quad(t\geq 0),

which implies that T⁡(t)​W0=W0T(t)W_{0}=W_{0} for all t≥0t\geq 0. Furthermore, Lemma 1 and the Pythagorean identity have been employed in order to see that

‖U0‖ℋ2≥‖U0‖ℋ2−‖W0‖ℋ2=‖V0‖ℋ2.\|U_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\geq\|U_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}-\|W_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\|V_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}.

∎

Remark 3

The stability of equilibria in Theorem 3.2 can also be reformulated in terms of the energy EU​(t)E_{U}(t) of every mild or classical solution to (1) - (4): Let U=U⁡(t,x)=[u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x),q⁡(t,x),θ⁡(t,x)]′U=U(t,x)=[u(t,x),v(t,x),q(t,x),\theta(t,x)]^{\prime} be a mild or classical solution to (1) - (4) with initial data U0=[u0,v0,q0,θ0,u1,v1]′∈ℋU_{0}=[u_{0},v_{0},q_{0},\theta_{0},u_{1},v_{1}]^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H} of the form U0=W0+V0U_{0}=W_{0}+V_{0}, where W0∈ker⁡(𝒜)W_{0}\in\operatorname{ker}(\mathcal{A}) and V0∈range⁡(𝒜)V_{0}\in\operatorname{range}(\mathcal{A}). Then there exist constants M>0M>0 and ω>0\omega>0, independent of the initial data, such that EU−W0​(t)≤M​e−ω​tE_{U-W_{0}}(t)\leq M\operatorname{e}^{-\omega t} for t≥0t\geq 0.

In (13, Corollary 3.9) the same model has been studied in a semilinear context and, without further explanations, the assumption

∫L1L2θ0​dx+m⁡(u01​(L2)−u01​(L1))=0,\displaystyle\int_{L_{1}}^{L_{2}}\theta_{0}\,dx+m(u^{1}_{0}(L_{2})-u^{1}_{0}(L_{1}))=0, (21)

has been imposed on the initial data.
